note: Two small fixes today, both about the office getting stuck or overspending when something goes wrong. The first is a real bug I found in our code: if the program closes while Serge is planning, that project can never be planned again.

questions: After a crash or a closed window, which of our 'in progress' states stay stuck forever (control_plane.mark_interrupted only covers two idea statuses)?
A claude -p worker can hang or run away. What do WORKER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=900 and --max-turns cover, and does Claude Code have a flag for a spend cap on one run?
If a worker run is stopped by a cap, does our code then pay for it a second time through the API fallback?
gaps: I did not test whether a killed claude -p run on Windows leaves child processes alive after subprocess.run times out (needs his PC). Python's own docs/issue 82388 shows the pipe-hang risk existed and was fixed in 3.7-3.9 for the direct child only.
No official page states whether --max-budget-usd counts the subscription 'API-equivalent' value the same way our usage table does; it says 'client-side cost estimate'.
I did not find a reliable measurement of how often claude -p hangs; only GitHub issues (anecdotes).

ideas.title: Never leave a plan stuck: reset 'planning' projects when the office starts
ideas.problem: control_plane.mark_interrupted() (called at server start, server.py:56) only fixes ideas in 'research' or 'judgment'. Serge's run sets the project to 'planning' (agents.py ~line 367) and only changes it when the run ends. If the window is closed or the PC restarts mid-plan, the project stays 'planning' forever. Then server.py ~806 and agents.py ~359 both refuse a new plan with 'This idea already has a plan (planning)'. The owner would see a plan that never finishes and cannot retry it from the office.
ideas.proposal: In control_plane.mark_interrupted(), also run: UPDATE projects SET status='error' WHERE status='planning' (use 'error', which agents.py already uses for a failed plan, so the UI already knows it). Add the count to the same 'halted' log line in server.py:56-58. Check that the office's retry path accepts 'error' (agents.py ~359 only blocks planning, awaiting_approval, approved, so it does). Same pass, nothing more: do not add heartbeats or timers.
ideas.gain: Removes one dead end the owner cannot fix without editing hq.db. About 3 lines of code. Measure: kill the server during a simulated plan, restart, and the idea can be planned again.
ideas.test: 1) Normal: start a simulated plan (HQ_SIMULATE=1 HQ_SIM_DELAY=5), stop the server after 2 s, restart: project shows 'error', the log says 1 interrupted, and 'Make a plan' works. 2) Edge: a project in 'awaiting_approval' or 'approved' at restart must stay unchanged. 3) Failure: two projects in 'planning' (one per idea) are both reset, count is 2.
ideas.confidence_why: Read directly from our own code on main (A): the status is written before the run and never reset on a crash. Weakest link: I did not run it; I traced it by reading.
ideas.risks: Very low. A run that is genuinely still going cannot exist at startup (the process just began), so resetting is safe. The 'error' status shows as failed, which is true.

ideas.title: Put a dollar cap on each worker run, and never pay for it twice
ideas.problem: workers.run() (workers.py:39-86) bounds a run by --max-turns (default 20) and a 900 s timeout (settings.WORKER_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), but not by spend. Measured typical runs are small (Vera $0.06, Serge $0.23, Sage short $0.15 in API-equivalent value), so a runaway run (many searches and page fetches) can cost many times that against the daily plan allowance before the next check. Also every worker failure is turned into workers.Unavailable, and agents.py (lines 128, 211, 421, 959, 1050, 1144) answers Unavailable by running the same job again through the paid API. A cap that simply raised Unavailable would therefore make a runaway run get paid twice.
ideas.proposal: 1) settings.py: WORKER_MAX_BUDGET_USD = {'Doulya': 0.60, 'Sage': 1.50, 'Vera': 0.50, 'Serge': 1.00, 'Calina': 2.00} (about 3-6x the measured typical run; the owner can edit in settings_local.py). 2) workers.run(): add '--max-budget-usd', str(cap) to cmd when the agent has a cap. 3) After the JSON is parsed, if out.get('subtype') == 'error_max_budget_usd', log a worker_budget_stop event (cost, turns) and raise a NEW exception workers.BudgetStop (not a subclass of Unavailable) so the caller does not fall back to the API; the office shows 'Sage stopped at the $1.50 cap' in Needs you. 4) Still call cp.record_usage() first so the spend counts toward the daily allowance (that code is already before the ok check).
ideas.gain: Puts a hard ceiling on the worst case of one run and makes it visible. Not a saving on normal days. Measure: worker_budget_stop events per week should be 0-1; if more, the cap is too tight and the owner is told which agent.
ideas.test: 1) Normal: a Vera run (about $0.06) finishes unchanged with --max-budget-usd 0.50. 2) Edge: set the cap to 0.01 for Vera in settings_local.py and run once for real: expect subtype error_max_budget_usd, a worker_budget_stop event, no API call (check the costs table), and the idea marked 'stopped', not retried. 3) Failure: the same stop for Sage mid-run must not write a half brief file.
ideas.confidence_why: The flag, its print-mode-only scope and 'client-side cost estimate' wording are from the official CLI reference (A); the post-call check and the error subtype come from two blog tests (B/C). Weakest link: unclear if the estimate matches our 'subscription value' numbers, and the final report is lost when the cap trips (one C source).
ideas.risks: The cap is checked after each API call, so a run can overshoot it by one call. A cap set too low would waste a run's work (the result is lost, tool effects stay). Needs one real run to confirm the exception path, which costs a few cents. If a cap is wrong, the owner can raise it in settings_local.py.
